opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes down to the stage we're at and the kind of work we do. Meshy is still a young company, and we're building something that sits right at the intersection of research, engineering, and product: 3D generative AI. That kind of work moves incredibly fast, and a lot of the most important progress happens in unplanned moments. Someone's looking at a weird artifact in a generated mesh, they turn to the person next to them, and in five minutes you've figured out it's a data issue, not a model issue. Remotely, that might take a day of Slack messages, or it just never happens because nobody wants to schedule a meeting for a half-formed thought.

I've also seen it from my own background. During my PhD at MIT, and when I was building Taichi, so much of what I learned came from just being around people who were smarter than me, overhearing discussions, getting pulled into whiteboard sessions. For early-career engineers especially, that osmosis is hard to replicate over Zoom. If we want people to grow quickly, and at a startup we need everyone to grow quickly, being together matters a lot.

And then there's speed and ownership. A startup's main advantage over big companies is iteration speed. When the team is in the same room, decisions happen faster, feedback loops are shorter, and there's a shared sense of urgency and energy that's hard to fake remotely.

That said, I don't think it's about control or counting hours. We keep one day flexible because people have lives, and deep focused work sometimes benefits from being at home. Four days is our balance: enough time together to keep that high-bandwidth collaboration and culture, with some flexibility built in. It's not the right answer for every company, but for a small team trying to push the frontier of 3D AI, I think it's the right one for us.

r001.rationale: The response says in-person conversations can resolve issues in five minutes, while remote discussion may take a day of Slack messages or never happen, and presents four days together as the balance that supports collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things people push back on, so let me explain how I think about it.

The honest answer is that Meshy is a startup trying to do something very hard. We're building generative AI for 3D, and that sits right at the intersection of research, graphics engineering, and product. Those three worlds don't naturally talk to each other. A researcher training a model, a graphics engineer worrying about mesh topology, and a designer thinking about what a game artist actually needs: they have to be in constant, messy, low-latency conversation. In my experience that kind of conversation just doesn't happen well over Slack or scheduled Zoom calls. It happens when someone walks over to your desk, you pull up a render together, and you figure it out in ten minutes instead of two days of async back-and-forth.

I also think about it from the perspective of speed. In this space, the window is short. The models are improving every few months, competitors are moving fast, and the difference between a team that iterates in hours versus days compounds enormously. When everyone is in the room, decisions get made faster, misunderstandings get caught faster, and you avoid that thing where two people quietly build toward different assumptions for a week.

And then there's the culture piece, which I think is underrated. A lot of what makes a small company work is trust and shared context, and that mostly gets built informally. Lunch conversations, overhearing a problem someone else is stuck on, a whiteboard session that nobody planned. Especially for newer or more junior people, being around experienced engineers is how you really learn. I benefited a lot from that kind of environment myself, and I want to give that to the team.

To be clear, I'm not dogmatic about it. One flexible day a week matters. People have lives, appointments, days where they just need to focus without interruption. And we try to make the office genuinely worth coming to, so it's not a "badge in and sit on video calls all day" situation. But for a company at our stage, with the kind of problem we're solving, I really do believe being together most of the time is a competitive advantage, not just a preference.

r001.rationale: The response says cross-functional discussion works better face to face than over Slack or scheduled Zoom, giving a ten-minute in-person resolution versus days of asynchronous back-and-forth.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main reason is communication. We’re working on something that requires a lot of experimentation, and it helps when people can sit together, look at the same result, and quickly exchange ideas. A small question can turn into a useful discussion without having to schedule a meeting.

I also think spending time together helps build trust and makes it easier for people to learn from one another. The four-day expectation gives us regular time for that collaboration while still leaving some flexibility. The goal is to help the team learn faster and build a better product together.

r001.rationale: The response says sitting together enables quick exchanges and useful discussions, but it does not state that Meshy found in-person discussion more efficient than remote discussion.

For me, it’s mainly about communication and iteration speed. We’re working on a product where AI research, engineering, and design need to come together. Being in the same room makes it easier to look at a result, notice something that isn’t working, and discuss how to improve it. Those small, spontaneous conversations can save a lot of back-and-forth.

I also think it helps people learn from each other and build trust, especially when someone is new. Four days gives us that regular time together while still leaving some flexibility. The point is to make it easier for the team to solve problems together.
